name: Proletarian internationalism
summary: Proletarian internationalism holds that capitalism is a world system and that workers of all nations share one class interest, so revolutions are parts of a single global struggle that should end in worldwide communism. It subordinates national loyalties to that class solidarity, opposes nationalism as the bourgeoisie's doctrine, and in the Leninist form demands the right of nations to self-determination and support for national liberation movements and among socialist states mutual assistance.
scope: The Marxist-Leninist doctrine of proletarian (later also 'socialist') internationalism as the Soviet-era textbooks s1 and s2 present it: the principle 'Workers of all countries, unite!' (the Communist Manifesto), Lenin's development of it for the imperialist era (the right of nations to self-determination up to secession, support for colonial liberation movements, the 1920 theses on the national and colonial questions for the Comintern), and its extension to relations among socialist states. s1 treats Trotskyites and 'Left' Communists as opponents of it, and Fainsod (s3) studies the pre-1919 'International Socialism' of the Second International as it broke apart in the First World War. The scope follows the defining sources' presentation of the doctrine, which is the official Soviet one; it does not make Trotskyist permanent revolution, Luxemburg's rejection of national self-determination or anarchist internationalism part of the profile, except where the sources discuss them as opponents.
